title: Integral closure of a one-dimensional Noetherian domain in a finite extension
statement: Let A be a Noetherian domain of Krull dimension 1 [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] with fraction field K, let L be a finite field extension of K, and let C be the integral closure of A in L [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Then C is a Dedekind domain (a Noetherian integrally closed domain of Krull dimension 1 [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]), and the map $\operatorname{Spec}(C) \to \operatorname{Spec}(A)$ is surjective with finite fibres and induces finite residue field extensions.

proof.text: Let D=C be the integral closure of A in L. Since A ⊆ C ⊆ L, the Krull–Akizuki theorem [lem-sc-krull-akizuki-noetherian] shows that C is Noetherian.

source.place: Algebra Lemma 09IG, first sentence, invoking Lemma 10.119.12 (Tag 00PG)

proof.text: The inclusion A → C is integral and injective, and C is a subring of the field L. Therefore the integral-extension dimension equality [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-dimension-equal] gives dim(C)=dim(A)=1. The integral closure C is integrally closed in L and is a domain, and its fraction field is L, by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-finite-extension-normal]. Hence C is a Noetherian integrally closed domain of dimension 1, i.e. a Dedekind domain.

source.place: Algebra Lemma 09IG, second and third sentences, invoking Lemmas 10.112.4 (Tag 00OK) and 10.120.17 (Tag 034X)

proof.text: The inclusion A ⊆ C is integral, so lying over [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-lying-over] says that every prime of A is the contraction of a prime of C. Thus Spec(C) → Spec(A) is surjective.

source.place: Algebra Lemma 09IG, fourth sentence, invoking Lemma 10.36.17 (Tag 00GQ)

proof.text: For a nonzero prime p of A, Ring.KrullDimLE 1 A makes p maximal. Since C is now Dedekind, Mathlib IsDedekindDomain.primesOver_finite gives finitely many prime ideals of C above p; the injective map from spectrum points to their ideals transports this finiteness to the scheme fibre. For the prime zero, Mathlib Ideal.eq_bot_of_comap_eq_bot shows that an ideal with zero contraction is zero: a nonzero integral element in the ideal would yield a nonzero base-ring element in its contraction. Thus the fibre is a singleton. The inclusion A to C is injective, so the contraction of zero is zero.

source.place: Tag 09IG, finite fibres; alternate Dedekind ideal-factorization argument, formalized using Mathlib IsDedekindDomain.primesOver_finite

proof.text: For a prime q of C whose contraction p is nonzero, q is nonzero and hence maximal in the Dedekind domain C. Choose a nonzero a in p. Using a finite K-basis of L, embed C A-linearly into K^r. Apply lem-sc-finite-length-global-submodule to its image to give finite A-length of C/aC. Since q is maximal, C to kappa(q) is surjective. As a belongs to p, aC maps to zero; the resulting quotient map C/aC to kappa(q) is A-linear and surjective. Thus kappa(q) is finite as an A-module. The canonical map kappa(p) to kappa(q) agrees with the A-action on ring elements, so restriction of scalars makes kappa(q) finite over kappa(p). If p=0, Mathlib Ideal.eq_bot_of_comap_eq_bot gives q=0. Both residue fields are fraction fields; their canonical map, by uniqueness on A, is the composite of a fraction-field isomorphism to K, the given finite map K to L, and a fraction-field isomorphism from L. It is therefore finite. Finally the canonical affine stalk isomorphisms conjugate the scheme residueFieldMap to the ideal ResidueField.map, preserving finiteness.
